newsitem.title: USA: Jazz drummer Tony Williams dies at 51.
newsitem.headline: Jazz drummer Tony Williams dies at 51.

text.p: Jazz drummer Tony Williams, who played with trumpeter Miles Davis as a teenager and became a ground-breaking musician himself, has died of a heart attack, his publicist said on Tuesday. He was 51.
Williams died at the Seton Medical Centre in Daly City, California, on Sunday afternoon, three days after he entered the hospital complaining of pains, publicist Kirk Tanksley said.
He had entered the hospital on Thursday, underwent minor gall bladder surgery on Friday and then spent two days recovering. "On Sunday he had chest pains and went into cardiac arrest," Tanksley said.

Williams was considered by musicians and critics alike one of the most inventive jazz drummers since the 1960s. He played with musicians as diverse as jazz legends John Coltrane and Thelonious Monk, rock superstars Jimi Hendrix and Bruce Springsteen and the avant-garde classical group, The Kronos Quartet.
Miles Davis, who already had an established reputation in 1963, tapped the drummer when he was only 17 to play in his band. "A drummer like Tony comes along only once in 30 years," Davis said.

Davis' group, which also included saxophonist Wayne Shorter, pianist Herbie Hancock and bassist Ron Carter, is still considered one of the greatest bands ever in jazz. A reunion album, "The Tribute to Miles Davis," with Wallace Roney on trumpet, was awarded a Grammy in 1995.

Williams was born December 12, 1945, in Chicago, Illinois, and was brought up in Boston. By the age of 8 he was playing the drums, and by 12 he was receiving private lessons from a teacher at the prestigious Berklee School of Music in Boston.
At age 14 he began to play professionally, but he got his big break in jazz in 1962 when he was asked to move to New York by the alto saxophonist Jackie McLean.

A year later he joined the Miles Davis band, and by the age of 18 received a solo recording contract from Blue Note Records and released his debut "Lifetime" -- the first avant-garde project released by the mainstream jazz label and also considered one of the earliest jazz fusion albums.
In 1969, he left Davis -- having recorded 13 albums with the trumpeter -- and went off on his own.

Since then he has recorded for Blue Note, Columbia Records, Polydor and most recently Ark 21 Records. His final release last year was "Wilderness," featuring guitarist Pat Metheny, saxophonist Michael Brecker, Hancock and bassist Stanley Clarke with a 30-piece orchestra.
Williams is survived by his wife Colleen and his mother, Alyse Janez. He lived in Pacifica, California, outside of San Francisco. Funeral services are pending.
